query: Many physical and chemical fabrication approaches have produced multi-element, near-equiatomic solid-solution nanoparticles, yet their synthesis–structure–property relationships remain poorly established. This limits evaluation of their suitability for catalytic operation at 773–1173 K and thermoelectric use at 473–1923 K, including catalytic settings where low noble-metal content is desirable. What governs whether these nanoparticles preserve structural and chemical stability under such service regimes, and why? Formulate one testable mechanistic hypothesis, specify a controlled intervention that separates it from competing explanations, predict observations relative to a baseline, define its boundary conditions, connect it to the prior evidence summarized above, and provide a clear falsification test.

generation.hypothesis: For multi-element, near-equiatomic solid-solution (high-entropy) nanoparticles, long-term structural and chemical stability at 773–1173 K is governed by whether the service temperature (T_service) remains below ~0.6 T_m,eff, where T_m,eff is the composition-weighted (“rule-of-mixtures”) melting point corrected for nanoscale depression. Introducing a small fraction (≤10 at %) of an ultra-refractory element (e.g., W or Ta) increases T_m,eff and the vacancy-formation / self-diffusion activation energy, thereby reducing atomic mobility and suppressing phase separation and coarsening. The key structural mediator is the bulk and surface self-diffusion coefficient (D) of the slowest constituent; raising the fraction of a high-melting, slow-diffusing element lowers D at a given temperature and preserves the single-phase solid solution.
generation.material_initial_state: ≈10 nm FCC NiCoFeCrMn (near-equiatomic) nanoparticles produced by inert-gas condensation, single-phase, chemically homogeneous.
generation.intervention: Substitute 5 at % of Fe with W (NiCoFe0.95W0.05CrMn) while keeping all other synthesis parameters identical.
generation.conditions: Isothermal anneal for 10 h in Ar at 1000 K (≈0.55 T_m,eff for W-doped; ≈0.7 T_m,eff for undoped) followed by quench to room temperature.
generation.structural_mediator: Bulk and surface self-diffusion coefficients governed by the highest vacancy-formation and migration barriers, set by the refractory element.
generation.mechanism: The added refractory element raises T_m,eff and the diffusion activation energy (Q) via stronger metallic bonding and larger atomic size, lowering D (D ∝ exp(−Q/RT)). When T_service < 0.6 T_m,eff, diffusion is too slow for significant compositional segregation or particle coalescence within the service time scale, so the configurational entropy stabilizes the single-phase structure. If T_service exceeds this threshold, diffusion accelerates, overcoming entropic stabilization and driving phase separation and Ostwald ripening.
generation.predicted_outcome: After annealing, W-doped nanoparticles remain single-phase FCC with <5 % change in lattice parameter and <10 % increase in average particle size, whereas undoped nanoparticles show (i) decomposition into Cr-rich α and Ni-Co-rich γ′ domains detectable by XRD peak splitting and STEM-EDS mapping and (ii) >50 % increase in average size due to coarsening.
generation.baseline: Undoped NiCoFeCrMn nanoparticles subjected to identical heat treatment serve as the baseline; they are expected to lose single-phase character and coarsen appreciably.
generation.boundary: Hypothesis applies to nanoparticles 5–30 nm in diameter, near-equiatomic compositions, and annealing temperatures ≤0.8 T_m,eff. It may fail for much larger particles (≥100 nm), for bulk samples, or when surface adsorbates drastically alter diffusion barriers.
generation.uncertainty: Magnitude of diffusion-barrier increase from 5 at % W is estimated; actual effect may depend on exact synthesis route and defect density. Surface segregation of W could reduce its bulk stabilizing impact.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare two nanoparticle batches (undoped and 5 at % W-doped) under identical inert-gas-condensation conditions. Anneal both at 1000 K for 10 h in flowing Ar, quench, then characterize phase constitution (XRD, synchrotron PDF), elemental distribution (STEM-EDS/EELS line scans), and particle size distribution (TEM). Measure self-diffusion coefficients via tracer studies or STEM-in-situ as feasible.
measurements: Tracer or in situ diffusion coefficients
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the W-doped nanoparticles display (a) comparable or greater phase separation/coarsening than the undoped batch OR (b) diffusion coefficients not significantly lower (≤10 %) than undoped at 1000 K, the hypothesis is falsified.
